title: From Ambiguous Requirements to Hallucinated Tests: A Multi-Domain Study of the Mirror Effect in LLM-Assisted Software Testing
content: Although large language models (LLMs) have the capacity to produce test cases rapidly, the accuracy of the test cases relies heavily on the specification given to the model. In this paper, we present Mirror Effect: an LLM is likely to reflect any level of clarity or ambiguity in natural-language requirements in subsequent test artifacts. For a comparative within-subjects experiment with five expert QA engineers, three commercial LLMs, four core requirements cases, and a five-domain transfer learning test, for each of the four core requirements, vague and measurable cases were formulated without altering the function, and then the two sets of prompts were compared against their human-generated baselines. As a result, four vague requirement prompts produced 127 test cases, 68% of which contained assumptions not present in the requirement statement, while four clear requirements produced 42 test cases with a hallucination rate of 12%. Coverage completeness improved from 42% to 92%, and mean QA review time reduced from 240 min to 85 min. As for the cross-domain experiments, the vague-prompt hallucination rate ranged from 68% to 88%, while for clear-requirement prompts, it ranged from 8% to 22%. Our findings are descriptive in nature due to the small sample size but demonstrate a consistent trend across all models and domains. In our contribution, we provide a definition of test hallucination using traceability, empirical evidence of ambiguity propagation, and a pre-prompt requirement gate.
